content: Meropenem/vaborbactam is indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTIs), including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible microorganisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterobacter cloacae species complex in adults aged 18 years and older. The recommended dosage is 4 grams (meropenem 2 grams/vaborbactam 2 grams) administered intravenously every 8 hours for up to 14 days, with each dose infused over 3 hours. Meropenem is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and patients with renal impairment may have an increased risk of adverse reactions. Geriatric patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, so dose adjustments and monitoring are advised. The safety and efficacy of this drug in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. Meropenem/vaborbactam reduces the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is contraindicated to administer live bacterial vaccines during antibiotic treatment; vaccination should be delayed until the antibiotic course is completed. Similarly, coadministration with the cholera vaccine should be avoided, as systemic antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination should not receive the cholera vaccine. This drug decreases the levels of divalproex sodium and valproic acid through an unknown mechanism, increasing the risk of seizures. If meropenem/vaborbactam is necessary, supplemental anticonvulsant therapy should be considered. It also reduces the efficacy of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores, as antibacterial agents may interfere with their activity. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Probenecid increases the levels of meropenem/vaborbactam by reducing its elimination through competition for active tubular secretion. Coadministration should be avoided, or alternative drugs should be considered. Drugs that inhibit OAT3 transporters may also increase seladelpar plasma concentrations, necessitating close monitoring. Meropenem/vaborbactam alters intestinal flora, which can reduce the effectiveness of oral forms of certain hormones, including conjugated estrogens, estradiol, and dienogest/estradiol valerate. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised, and alternative or additional forms of birth control may be recommended during concurrent use. Similarly, the drug may increase the levels of digoxin by altering intestinal flora, requiring careful monitoring. The drug may also reduce the levels or effects of certain vitamins, such as biotin, niacin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, thiamine, and vitamin K1 (phytonadione), by altering intestinal flora. These interactions are generally minor, but their clinical significance is unknown. Meropenem/vaborbactam decreases the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of the vaccine should be delayed until the antibiotic course is completed. The drug is excreted in human milk, but it is unknown whether vaborbactam is excreted. The effects on breastfed infants or milk production are not well studied. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the infant. For preparation and administration, the diluted solution of meropenem/vaborbactam should have a final concentration of 2–8 mg/mL. The solution should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration before use; it should appear colorless to light yellow. Any unused portion should be discarded. The diluted solution should be infused intravenously over 3 hours and must be used within 4 hours if stored at room temperature or within 22 hours if refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F). Unopened vials should be stored at room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F), with permissible excursions to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Reconstituted vials or diluted solutions can be stored for 4 hours at room temperature or 22 hours if refrigerated. This information is provided for general educational purposes. For the most current and specific details, consult prescribing information or contact the applicable healthcare provider.
